# **Regularized High-Dimensional Covariance & Spectrum Estimation:** Main Method Families

When the number of variables exceeds or rivals the number of samples, the sample covariance is rank-deficient or ill-conditioned and its eigenvalues are heavily biased. Research has developed several regularization strategies that either impose structure on the covariance or directly correct the eigenvalue spectrum, often with the goal of recovering population eigenvalues.

## **Main Classes of Regularized Covariance Estimators**  

### **1. Structured (Model-Based) Covariance Estimation**  
- **Tapering/banding:** Enforce approximate banded structure (e.g., time/space ordering) and often combine with shrinkage toward identity, such as the **Tabasco** tapered–shrinkage estimator for low n/p ratios  (Lam, 2019; Karoui, 2006).  
- **Factor / spiked covariance models:** Use low-rank plus noise structure and adjust eigenvalues/eigenvectors; examples include S-POET for spiked models and factor-based methods  (Lam, 2019; Wang & Fan, 2017).  
- These methods improve conditioning and can target interpretable structure but rely on correct model assumptions  (Lam, 2019; Karoui, 2006; Bartz, 2016).  

### **2. Shrinkage Toward Simple Targets (Linear / Polynomial Shrinkage)**  
- **Linear shrinkage (Ledoit–Wolf and extensions):** Shrink sample covariance toward a multiple of the identity (or other targets) with analytically chosen weights to minimize mean squared error, effective in “large p, small n” and under elliptical distributions  (Lam, 2019; Won et al., 2013; Zhang et al., 2022; Ollila & Raninen, 2018; Chen et al., 2010).  
- **Higher-order Stein-type shrinkage:** Model the estimator as a polynomial in the sample covariance and a target matrix, optimized via convex MSE criteria to yield well-conditioned estimators  (Ledoit & Wolf, 2012).  
- **Condition-number regularization:** Directly constrain the condition number using a likelihood-based approach, yielding a Steinian-type shrinkage estimator  (Won et al., 2013).  

### **3. Rotation-Invariant / Eigenvalue-Shrinkage Methods**  

| Goal | Typical Approach | Population spectrum link | Citations |
|------|------------------|--------------------------|-----------|
| Better eigenspectrum | Nonlinear shrinkage of sample eigenvalues (keep eigenvectors) | Uses large‑dimensional random matrix theory; approximates oracle eigenvalue map |  (Lam, 2019; Won et al., 2013; Ledoit & Wolf, 2020; Jain et al., 2023; Ledoit & Wolf, 2020)|
| Direct spectrum recovery | Solve a Marčenko–Pastur–based inverse problem for eigenvalue distribution | Estimates population eigenvalue distribution via convex optimization, then recovers eigenvalues |  (Lam, 2019; Karoui, 2006; Jain et al., 2023; Banerjee & Monni, 2021)|
| Optimal shrinkers in spiked models | Design loss-specific optimal eigenvalue shrinkers | Closed forms under spiked covariance asymptotics |  (Wang & Fan, 2017; Donoho et al., 2013)|
| Moment-based spectrum estimation | Recover moments then eigenvalues (even n ≪ p) | Gives finite-sample error bounds, consistent even when n/p→0 |  (Kong & Valiant, 2016)|

**Figure 1:** Key eigenvalue-based methods for spectrum estimation

Rotation-invariant approaches are central for **recovering the underlying eigenvalue spectrum**: they explicitly model the link between sample and population eigenvalues using random matrix theory (Marčenko–Pastur) and/or spiked models  (Wang & Fan, 2017; Karoui, 2006; Ledoit & Wolf, 2020; Jain et al., 2023; Kong & Valiant, 2016; Banerjee & Monni, 2021; Donoho et al., 2013).  

### **4. Bayesian and Robust Shrinkage**  
- **Bayesian gSIW prior:** Generalized shrinkage inverse-Wishart priors give posterior-consistent eigenvalues/eigenvectors under spiked covariance, even when p/n→∞  (Kim et al., 2025).  
- **Robust shrinkage (Tyler-type):** Regularized robust estimators handle heavy-tailed elliptical data and remain usable in n < p, with MMSE-based shrinkage selection  (Chen et al., 2010).  

## **Summary**  

Well-established tools include (i) structural regularizers (factor, tapering/banding), (ii) shrinkage toward simple targets (linear or higher-order), (iii) rotation-invariant eigenvalue shrinkage and spectrum inversion using Marčenko–Pastur and spiked models, and (iv) Bayesian and robust shrinkage priors. For **eigenvalue spectrum recovery**, nonlinear eigenvalue shrinkage and random-matrix-based spectrum estimators are the main workhorses, often providing consistent population eigenvalue estimates even when the sample covariance is rank-deficient.
